items.title: Mean formulas
items.content: For \(n\) observations, arithmetic mean \(=\frac{\text{sum}}{n}\). Therefore sum \(=n\times\text{mean}\). Combined mean \(=\frac{n_1m_1+n_2m_2}{n_1+n_2}\). A weighted mean is \(\frac{\sum wx}{\sum w}\).

items.title: Choose the correct denominator
items.content: Use the number of observations, not the number of categories, unless each category has one observation. Weighted values count according to their frequency or weight.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Check a computed mean by multiplying it by the count to recover the total.
The mean is sensitive to every observation and can be affected by extreme values.

items.title: Arithmetic mean
items.content: Worked example: mean of 5, 8, 11, and 16 is \(40/4=10\). The mean need not be one of the observed values.

items.title: Recovering a total
items.content: Worked example: 12 students have mean score 68, so their total is \(12\times68=816\) marks.

items.title: Missing observation
items.content: Worked example: five numbers have mean 14, so total is 70. If four sum to 51, the missing number is \(70-51=19\).

items.title: Combined average
items.content: Worked example: 10 learners average 60 and 20 learners average 75. Combined mean is \( (10\cdot60+20\cdot75)/30=70\).

items.title: Weighted average
items.content: Worked example: 2 kg at ₹30/kg and 3 kg at ₹50/kg cost ₹210 for 5 kg. Average price is \(210/5=₹42\) per kg.

items.title: Effect of adding or removing data
items.content: Adding a value above the old mean raises the mean; adding one below lowers it. Worked example: a mean of 10 over four values gives total 40; adding 15 yields \(55/5=11\).

items.title: Find mean from observations
items.content: Add every observation once, then divide by the count. Worked example: 4, 6, 9 have mean \(19/3\).

items.title: Find total from mean and count
items.content: Worked example: mean 23 for 8 items gives total \(23\times8=184\).

items.title: Find a missing value
items.content: Worked example: mean of 6 values is 12; five sum to 67. Missing value is \(72-67=5\).

items.title: Combine two groups
items.content: Use group totals, not the unweighted average of group means. Worked example: group sizes 5 and 15 with means 40 and 60 give \( (200+900)/20=55\).

items.title: Weighted rate or price
items.content: Multiply each rate by its quantity, add, then divide by total quantity. This applies to average speed only when distance/time details support that weighting. Worked example: 2 kg at ₹30/kg and 3 kg at ₹50/kg cost ₹210 total, so the weighted mean is ₹42/kg.

items.title: Derive the missing-value rule
items.content: From \(m=S/n\), multiply both sides by \(n\): \(S=nm\). Subtract the known values from \(S\) to get a missing observation.

items.title: Derive combined mean
items.content: Group 1 total is \(n_1m_1\), group 2 total is \(n_2m_2\). Add totals and divide by the combined count \(n_1+n_2\).

items.title: Why group means are not usually averaged directly
items.content: A mean of a large group represents more observations. The combined total must weight each group mean by its group size.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Wrong count
items.content: Count all observations, including repeated values; frequency tables require multiplying each value by its frequency.

items.title: Averaging group averages equally
items.content: Use a weighted mean when group sizes differ.

items.title: Confusing total and mean
items.content: Mean is a per-observation value; recover the total by multiplying by the count.

items.title: Rounding too early
items.content: Keep exact sums or fractions through intermediate steps, then round only if requested.

keyTakeaways: Mean equals total divided by count.
Combined averages are weighted by group size.
Frequency tables use value multiplied by frequency.
